newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-ITALY CONSIDERS ENGLISH-STYLE HOOLIGAN POLICING.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ITALY CONSIDERS ENGLISH-STYLE HOOLIGAN POLICING.

text.p: Italy said on Thursday that it was studying an English-style crackdown on soccer hooliganism as police in Florence said 24 fans faced charges over violence at last Sunday's Fiorentina-Juventus tie.

The idea of emulating England's police and club assault on the hooliganism that besmirched the game in the 1980s emerged from a two-hour summit of soccer authorities with Italy's police chief Fernando Masone and deputy prime minister Walter Veltroni.

"We are studying a package of initiatives that in part will follow the example of England, where they have managed to resolve the problem of hooligans," Italian soccer league chief Franco Carraro told reporters.
"The aim is to prevent the ills of Italian society from finding an outlet through acts of violence inside the stadium," he said.
Italian soccer has faced a mounting problem of violence in recent years, much of it from youths linked to extreme right groups.

Fighting in Florence last weekend left 20 policemen and fans injured and included a stone-throwing attack on the Juventus team bus as it arrived at the stadium for the match, which ended in a 1-1 draw. Windows were smashed but no players were hurt.
Police on Thursday said they had identified 24 Fiorentina fans who would face charges of assault and criminal damage, 11 of them in connection with the bus attack.
Those disturbances came one week after Reggiana fans hurled four kilos of metal objects including a bathroom tap at the Parma goal during the clubs' local derby.

England, infamous for its soccer-related violence at home and abroad during the 1980s, has made great strides in keeping the trouble under control through sophisticated stadium surveillance, police escort methods and the work of its undercover police National Football Intelligence Unit.
Calls for Italy to learn the English lesson have grown as violence has persisted.
Carraro said the aim of soccer authorities was to keep the peace among fans and "to make football a family game again".
"I believe that it could be a winning package," he said.
"In England, where there is a violent society, they have resolved the problem of hooligans with similar methods. Why can't we?" he asked.
Published statistics show 871 police and fans were injured in clashes last season and that this season's injury toll is already above 300.

In January 1995, the fatal stabbing of a Genoa fan by a supporter of rival club AC Milan jolted Italy and brought the national game to a halt for one Sunday to signal the intent to stamp down on hooliganism.
The fan responsible for the knifing, teenager Simone Barbaglia, is serving an 11 year and four month jail sentence for wilful murder.
